Legacy building control systems may have some, but not all, of the capabilities found in modern smart systems. They may have outdated or proprietary equipment, or components that are incompatible with newer devices or communication protocols, limiting integration and advanced control strategies. In contrast, most newer, smart devices can share a common concern: cybersecurity. The rapid proliferation of con- nected technologies, combined with little standardization across products, creates challenges for building operators and Information Technology (IT) teams. Without consistent security protocols or interoperability guidelines, it can be difficult to implement a comprehensive cybersecurity regimen. Effective strategies often require a combination of device-level security features, network segmentation, regular software updates, and integration with broader building or enterprise cybersecurity polices. 2.1.4 Building-Grid Interface Equipment Grid interface devices serve as the critical connection points between building systems and the electrical grid. While these devices are part of the broader grid infrastructure (discussed further in Section 3.2), their integration with build- ing management systems presents unique challenges and opportunities from a building perspective. As buildings become more energy-aware and seek to optimize their grid interactions, the capabilities of these interface devices become increasingly important for building operations. • Legacy Meterscan require manual reading by utility personnel and provide no real-time information to build- ing operators. This limits a building’s ability to monitor energy consumption patterns, identify inefficiencies, or respond to time-of-use pricing signals. Without access to granular consumption data, building management systems cannot optimize operations based on actual energy usage or costs. • Smart Meterscan be read remotely and enable real-time monitoring of electricity consumption, allowing building systems to respond dynamically to usage patterns and pricing signals. Advanced smart meters can provide interval data that helps building operators understand load profiles and optimize equipment schedul- ing. However, integration capabilities vary significantly, and many smart meters still provide limited direct communication with building management systems, requiring additional gateway devices or software inter- faces. • Legacy Invertersfor on-site renewable generation (primarily solar PV systems) often function as simple power conversion devices with minimal communication capabilities. From a building energy management per- spective, these legacy inverters provide no visibility into generation performance, system health, or real-time production data. Building operators cannot integrate solar generation information into their energy manage- ment strategies, potentially missing opportunities to optimize self-consumption or coordinate generation with building loads. • Smart Invertersprovide real-time generation monitoring, system performance analytics, and integration capa- bilities with building automation systems. Smart inverters can enable buildings to maximize self-consumption of on-site generation, coordinate solar production with controllable loads, and even provide grid services while optimizing building energy costs. Some smart inverters support energy storage integration, allowing buildings to further optimize their grid interactions through strategic charging and discharging of battery systems. The evolution from legacy to smart grid interface devices represents a fundamental shift in how buildings can inter- act with the electrical grid and other utilities.
